title: A Guide to Sherwood
intro: A spoiler-free reminder of who's who and where's where in Robin Hood and His Merry Messes. Updated as new faces and places show up in the stories.

entries.name: Robin of Loxby
entries.kind: an archer of middling skill
entries.blurb: Earnest, well-meaning, and a genuinely terrible shot with a bow — which has, so far, worked out better for him than it has any right to. Estranged from his father, though he'd rather not talk about it.

entries.name: Long John Little
entries.kind: a very large, very apologetic man
entries.blurb: Enormous, gentle, and bad at being intimidating no matter how the job description reads. Recently found himself running in the same direction as Robin, for reasons that seemed sensible at the time.

entries.name: Will Scarlett-Sleeves
entries.kind: a man of considerable debt and excellent posture
entries.blurb: Vain, charming, and perpetually broke in a manner entirely of his own making. Owns exactly one truly fine garment, and would very much like you to notice it.

entries.name: Brother Crumb
entries.kind: a friar with strong opinions on charity
entries.blurb: Left his abbey over a disagreement about how generous generosity ought to be. Cooks better than anyone has a right to, and always seems to have more food on hand than the sack should allow.

entries.name: Abbot Percival
entries.kind: a patient man reaching the end of his patience
entries.blurb: Still technically Brother Crumb's superior, a fact he brings up more often than it helps. Not unkind, not a villain — just a man who preferred caution to the kind of charity his kitchener had in mind.

entries.name: Marian Fletcher
entries.kind: the only one of them who has a plan
entries.blurb: Runs a fletcher's shop with a sideline in quiet, deniable mercy. Sharp, exhausted, and entirely too clever to have needed rescuing by anyone.

entries.name: Master Thistlewood
entries.kind: an old man of unusual competence
entries.blurb: A great many books, a great many opinions, and a walking staff he uses with more skill than any old man reasonably should. Turned up at exactly the right moment once, which everyone has decided to be grateful for rather than curious about. Mostly.

entries.name: Pip
entries.kind: Thistlewood's grandson
entries.blurb: Quiet, quick, and considerably more capable in a fight than a boy his age has any business being. Keeps his own counsel. Mended a ruined sleeve well enough that nobody asked too many questions about how.

entries.name: Ferret Tam
entries.kind: a trader with flexible ethics
entries.blurb: The man Will owes money to. Not unreasonable, exactly, just very serious about invoices — and about the unusual angles a debt can be viewed from.

entries.name: Agnes Hale
entries.kind: a woman who does not need rescuing, thank you
entries.blurb: Runs her household with a sharp tongue and zero patience for anyone's nonsense, including the outlaws who keep turning up to ‘help.’

entries.name: Wat Hale
entries.kind: Agnes's son, and a natural opportunist
entries.blurb: Nine years old and already better than most adults at spotting the exact moment to grab back what's yours.

entries.name: Tom Weaver
entries.kind: a weaver whose home is also his livelihood
entries.blurb: Steady, quietly proud of what he's built with his own hands — which makes the notice sitting on his table considerably harder to look at.

entries.name: Hob Weaver
entries.kind: Wat's friend, and unexpectedly decisive for nine
entries.blurb: Knew exactly who to go to when his family's roof came under threat. Wasn't wrong to.

entries.name: Vane
entries.kind: a man who bought the right to be a problem
entries.blurb: Purchased the tax-collection rights for a whole district, and has been finding creative new dwellings-related reasons to exercise them ever since.

entries.name: The Sheriff of Nottingham
entries.kind: a man who has started asking questions
entries.blurb: Hasn't crossed paths with the crew directly yet — but a run of tax men, highwaymen, and suspiciously warped arrows has caught his attention. Word is he doesn't like coincidences.

entries.name: Sherwood
entries.kind: a forest, mostly
entries.blurb: Large, green, and short on both witnesses and tax collectors — two qualities Robin has come to appreciate.

entries.name: The Abbey
entries.kind: Brother Crumb's former posting
entries.blurb: A well-stocked, well-meaning, occasionally over-cautious institution. Its larder has been mysteriously generous to the surrounding villages for about a year now — the Abbot has recently worked out why.

entries.name: Thistlewood's Cottage
entries.kind: cluttered, and somehow all the better for it
entries.blurb: Books stacked two deep, herbs drying from every beam, and an unusual amount of hospitality for two people who claim to be simply passing through.

entries.name: Nottingham
entries.kind: the town everyone's trying not to end up in
entries.blurb: Market stalls, cobbled streets, and a Sheriff who has recently developed an active interest in a certain string of coincidences.

entries.name: The Geese Village
entries.kind: small, unlucky, and not actually named that
entries.blurb: Nobody remembers its real name anymore — not since the geese. Home to Agnes and Wat Hale, and the place where all of this, one way or another, started.

entries.name: Gideon
entries.kind: a goat of strong opinions
entries.blurb: Level-headed right up until he isn't. No one has ever caught him eating the laundry directly, which everyone finds more suspicious than reassuring.

entries.name: Grimalkin
entries.kind: an old tomcat who has seen enough, thank you
entries.blurb: Aloof to nearly everyone, and inexplicably devoted to exactly one person. Marian hasn't decided yet whether that's flattering or concerning.

entries.name: Barley
entries.kind: a young dog with excellent priorities
entries.blurb: Loves everyone who has hands, and most things that involve bread. Fiercer than he looks, when it matters.

entries.name: What is cant?
entries.kind: local slang
entries.blurb: A rhyming turn of phrase used throughout Sherwood and Nottingham — the phrase's last word rhymes with what it actually means. Everyone seems to understand it. Everyone, notably, except Robin.

entries.name: Bell and book
entries.kind: means “crook” (a thief)
entries.blurb: On account of ‘book’ rhyming with ‘crook.’ As in: watch your purse, there's bell-and-books about.

entries.name: Candle wax
entries.kind: means “tax”
entries.blurb: As in: candle wax, season on season, till there was nothing left to smith for.

entries.name: Pig in a poke
entries.kind: means “broke” (penniless)
entries.blurb: As in: thoroughly pig-in-a-poke at present, haven't a coin to my name.

entries.name: Friar's hood
entries.kind: means “good”
entries.blurb: As in: proper friar's-hood, that decision. Best I've made in years. (Yes, someone had to point out the irony to a literal friar.)

entries.name: Hound's tooth
entries.kind: means “truth”
entries.blurb: As in: a hound's-tooth's worth of resistance, and no more.

entries.name: Beggar's cloak
entries.kind: means “joke”
entries.blurb: As in: you are a beggar's-cloak of a thief, you know that? (Said with real affection, to a dog, about a stolen loaf of bread.)
